edges.effect_quant: The most reproducible benefit of early-life probiotics is a reduction in eczema risk, while protection against the broader basket of allergic disease is much less consistent.
edges.population: pregnant women, breastfeeding mothers, and infants receiving probiotic interventions for allergy prevention
edges.mechanism: Probiotics can alter early gut colonization and train mucosal immune responses during a developmental window when allergic sensitization is still plastic. That mechanism fits eczema prevention better than it fits a broad claim that all allergic disease is meaningfully reduced.
edges.summary: This is not a blanket anti-allergy effect. The best evidence says probiotics modestly reduce eczema risk in early life, especially in high-risk infants and when given across the mother-infant window, but they do not reliably prevent every allergic outcome in the same way.
edges.caveats: Strain, timing, and host risk profile matter a great deal here. The safest interpretation is that probiotics may help shift the broad allergic-disease burden downward a little, mainly through eczema prevention, rather than acting as a universal allergy shield.

evidence.citation: Wang HZ et al 2025 Cochrane Database Syst Rev
